Photograph: Baltimore Sun/TNS Texas University of Maryland ‘teacher of the year’ detained by ICE in Texas DHS said pharmacy instructor Berhanu Kibret overstayed visa and arrested him at Dallas-Fort Worth airport Maya Yang Tue 4 Aug 2026 15.11 EDT Last modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 15.12 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An instructor at the University of Maryland, Baltimore who only just received a “teacher of the year” award has been arrested by federal immigration agents under the command of the Trump administration . Immigration and Customs Enforcement ( ICE ) officials detained Berhanu Kibret, an instructor at the university’s pharmacy school, at the Dallas-Fort Worth airport in Texas, according to multiple news reports. The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, confirmed Kibret’s arrest, citing an expired visa – but it stopped short of providing a location. In a statement, the University of Maryland said Kibret was arrested while returning from a meeting of the American Association of Colleges of Pharmacy, where he received a “teacher of the year” award. Immigrant being held at Delaney Hall dies, marking 22nd death in ICE custody Read more “Dr Kibret has a valid work authorization, so it is our hope that any issues surrounding his status will be quickly resolved and that he will be permitted to continue his work at the University of Maryland School of Pharmacy,” the institution added, according to CBS. Kibret’s research focuses on how the brain’s cannabinoid system influences mental health, brain disease and the effects of addictive drugs, the university’s website says. He obtained bachelor’s and master’s degrees in science as well as a PhD in Ethiopia – and he completed his postdoctoral fellowship at William Paterson University in Wayne, New Jersey. Calling Kibret a “highly valued member of the University of Maryland, Baltimore community”, the school said it was “greatly troubled” by his arrest. The university added: “He is an effective and beloved teacher, and a highly regarded colleague. His detention has generated not only great sympathy for his plight, but also a heightened sense of apprehension here on campus.” In a statement to the Guardian, the DHS said ICE arrested Kibret after he entered the US on 21 June 2021 on a visa set to expire on 31 May 2024. “Against our nation’s laws, he overstayed his visa and failed to depart,” the DHS statement said. “He will remain in ICE custody pending his immigration proceedings.” The Guardian has reached out to the University of Maryland, Baltimore for additional comment. Arrests such as that of Kibret have drawn criticism, particularly in light of the Trump administration’s repeated pledge to focus on targeting the “worst of the worst criminal illegal aliens” for arrest and deportation. A Guardian analysis published in February found that 77% of people placed into deportation proceedings for the first time after Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025 had no criminal convictions. Kibret’s arrest came after ICE in July detained and later released a Johns Hopkins researcher at the Baltimore/Washington international airport. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Around 2-3 times a day Sign up to Breaking News US Get the most important news as it breaks Preview latest after newsletter promotion Federal authorities detained Fatima Ameaka, a Cameroonian citizen with a doctorate in pharmacy who works at Johns Hopkins University’s Bloomberg School of Public Health. Speaking to several outlets during Ameaka’s detention, a Johns Hopkins spokesperson described her as a “respected member of our community”. “The university understands the fear and concern this instills in members of our community,” the spokesperson added. “Dr Ameaka was traveling in a personal capacity, and though we cannot comment on the specifics of her situation, we want to assure our community that the university is actively working to provide support for Dr Ameaka, including ensuring she has access to legal representation.” Documents reviewed by ABC indicated that Ameaka held a work authorization valid through 2029 and had a pending asylum case. Nonetheless, as ABC reported , the DHS had initially said of Ameaka: “In violation of our nation’s laws, she overstayed her visa. She will remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings.” Ameaka’s attorney on Sunday confirmed that she had been released from ICE detention. https://www.politico.eu/article/king-cha.text: LONDON — King Charles has invited leading figures from the artificial intelligence industry to an exclusive event set to take place this month, according to two people familiar with the plans who were granted anonymity because it has yet to be publicly announced. The event is scheduled to be held in Dumfries House in Ayrshire, Scotland — the headquarters of The King’s Foundation, a charity founded by Charles in 1990 to advocate on environmental and social issues, the two people said. According to one of the people, the exclusive gathering's guest list is set to include Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang, British founder of Google DeepMind Demis Hassabis and Paolo Benanti, an adviser to the Vatican on AI. Advertisement Advertisement That person said around 30 high-profile people from the AI industry were invited to attend in total. A Royal official told POLITICO: “One of the king’s unique abilities as sovereign and global statesmen is his ability to convene top level stakeholders.” The official stressed King Charles would not issue his own thoughts, but wants to “convene, engage, listen and encourage debate” on one of the biggest issues of the age. The event is being organized by the Ditchley Foundation — a charity which organizes discussions on global issues, and ministers will also be invited. Benanti declined to comment. Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment. A representative for Google DeepMind said they could not comment on Hassabis’ movements. Hassabis, who is now chair of DeepMind, in July called for the creation of a U.S.-based global standards organization for AI. Advertisement Advertisement King Charles has also shown an interest in the development and regulation of AI. The king met Nvidia’s Huang and tech executives from Apple, Amazon and Google during a state visit to Washington in April, where he highlighted collaboration on AI between the U.S. and U.K. He also hosted a banquet at Windsor Castle during President Donald Trump’s state visit to the U.K. last September which was attended by tech industry leaders including Huang and OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman. Trump’s visit coincided with the announcement of significant investment in the U.K. by U.S. tech firms and the signing of a U.S.-U.K. Tech Prosperity Deal, which was later suspended over trade disagreements. In November, Huang and other pioneers in AI received an award from King Charles, and the Nvidia chief executive said the king gifted him a copy of an address he made at the AI Safety Summit which said: “If we are to realize the untold benefits of AI, then we must work together in combatting its significant risks.” This story has been updated to include a quote from a Royal official. https://www.dw.com/en/berlin-businesswom.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MYcu Prosecutors say the Russian intelligence officer whom Ilona W. allegedly assisted was based at the Russian Embassy in Berlin Image: Michael Bihlmayer/CHROMORANGE/picture alliance Advertisement German federal prosecutors have charged a 57-year-old Berlin businesswoman with carrying out intelligence activities for Russia . Ilona W., who holds German and Ukrainian citizenship, is accused of working for the intelligence service of a foreign power, according to the Federal Prosecutor's Office. She was arrested on January 21 and remains in pre-trial detention. What is Ilona W. accused of? Prosecutors say Ilona W. ran a marketing agency in Berlin and also chaired a lobbying association, giving her extensive contacts in military and political circles. She allegedly had contact with a full-time Russian intelligence officer at the Russian Embassy in Berlin from at least October 2023. According to the indictment, she repeatedly supplied him with information about high-profile events and helped arrange access for him, in some cases under a false name. Berlin detains German-Ukrainian woman for Russian espionage To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Prosecutors say the aim was to allow the Russian intelligence officer to build up his own network for intelligence purposes. What information was she allegedly seeking? Ilona W. is also accused of attending events herself to identify useful contacts and potential targets. Prosecutors say she tried to recruit people from Germany's Defense Ministry and the arms industry. She also allegedly sought information on German defense policy and the defense industry on behalf of her Russian contact, particularly in connection with Russia's war against Ukraine. The charges were filed last week before the state security division of Berlin's Higher Regional Court. Germany expelled the suspected Russian intelligence officer linked to the case shortly after W.'s arrest, prompting Moscow to retaliate by expelling a German diplomat. https://www.dw.com/en/how-trump-s-diesel.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OEq4 Donald Trump now allows Russian diesel imports into the US Image: Eric Lee/REUTERS Advertisement Many Ukrainians and Europeans viewed news from Washington over the past weekend as a stab in the back by their US ally. First, President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel, which involves a temporary easing of US sanctions against Moscow. And later Trump announced an allegedly agreed "energy ceasefire" between Ukraine and Russia. Kyiv said the idea had not been discussed with Ukraine, but that it was prepared to halt attacks on Russia's energy infrastructure if Moscow did the same. 'Trump is not interested in supporting Ukraine' Security expert Carlo Masala of the Bundeswehr University Munich said the developments showed that "Trump is not interested in supporting Ukraine at all, but that domestic US politics and relations with Russia are far more important to him than supporting Ukraine." He added that the president aims to sway the outcome of the US midterm elections on November 3 through an agreement with Russia. All seats in the House of Representatives and a regularly scheduled portion of the Senate will be contested in the midterm elections. Polls suggest that Trump's Republican Party could lose its majority in the House. A loss of the Republicans' Senate majority is also possible. Surveys indicate that American voters are unhappy with high fuel prices, and the US president apparently hopes to influence prices through diesel shipments from Russia. Can Trump’s diesel deal bring down US fuel prices? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Observers, however, consider Trump's hopes that Russian diesel shipments could affect prices in the US illusory. "The volume is so small that it will have absolutely no effect on prices," Thomas Jäger of the University of Cologne told German public broadcaster ARD . The political scientist added that shipments planned before the midterm elections would not even cover US diesel demand for a single day. "The same applies to any shipments that may arrive afterward, if they materialize, they will have no effect on prices either," he said. Trump's goal, Jäger said, is simply "the story" — showing voters that he is trying to solve a problem that matters to them. 'No concrete military benefits for Russia' The main criticism from Kyiv and EU countries is that Russia will use the revenue from diesel sales to finance its war against Ukraine . Carlo Masala, however, does not foresee the agreement with the US having "any concrete positive military effects" for Russia. He points out that Washington had already temporarily suspended sanctions on Russian oil exports in March this year, shortly after the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran . "Despite the money Russia has and has received, it has no military strategy for making further advances in the Donbas. The issue is more about the political impact and the symbolism of the Americans striking separate deals with the Russians at Ukraine's expense," the expert said. Another cause for concern in Kyiv could be US threats to suspend intelligence sharing with Ukraine and block the PURL (Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List) program unless Ukraine halts its attacks on Russian oil refineries. Under the PURL program, European countries procure US weapons for Ukraine. Trump, Russia and Ukraine: Has the US changed sides again? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video European alternatives to US intelligence A possible US decision to stop sharing intelligence with Ukraine for strikes on Russian territory would have "dramatic" consequences for Kyiv, Masala said, but European intelligence, particularly from France, could help mitigate the impact. While French intelligence is "not as comprehensive as American intelligence," the Ukrainian military already uses it to carry out strikes in Russia with French weapons systems. As for the weapons European countries procure from the US for Ukraine under the PURL program, Masala noted that the program's most important component — interceptor missiles for air defense — has barely been available to Ukraine since the start of the war with Iran. Support for Ukraine across both US parties Ahead of the US midterm elections, experts point out that Ukraine enjoys broad support not only among Democrats but also among Republicans. One example is the bipartisan passage this summer of legislation to tighten US sanctions against Russia , known as the "Lindsey Graham Act," named after its Republican congressional sponsor , who has since died. Signed by Trump in September, the law gives the president a broad range of tools. He can impose sanctions on Russian officials, oligarchs, financial institutions and Russia's shadow fleet, which is used to circumvent restrictions on oil exports. He can also impose punitive tariffs on buyers of Russian energy products. There is broad bipartisan support for Ukraine in US Congress Image: Valerio Rosati/Visually/picture alliance "Trump may resist, but political forces, particularly after the US midterms, may push the administration in the direction of trying to seek an end to the war by using the tools available," former US diplomat Daniel Fried told DW. He added that the "Lindsey Graham Act" and the 2022 law banning US imports of Russian oil are "not absolute, but strong barriers against dumb ideas like a unilateral unrequited diesel deal with Russia." Several Democratic and Republican senators cited this legislation in a joint statement in which they described the diesel deal with Russia as illegal, calling on the US government to "immediately correct" its decision.
